## TL;DR

The phone Work queue now opens on a grouped "Needs attention" view instead of
1,065 cards sorted newest-first. Needs-you, Review, Active, Ready and Inbox
sections render before anything done; Done only appears behind its own filter or
last in "All statuses". The queue gained an inline search (id, title, area),
quick chips (priority, area, story, human assignment, plus Held / Archived /
Human shortcuts), URL-backed filter and search state (`?status=`, `?q=`,
`?priority=`, `?area=`, `?story=`, `?mine=`, `?sort=`), and section pagination
(12 cards initially) with `content-visibility` so a 1,000-task board stays
cheap to paint. Held, archived and human tasks are now first-class queue views,
reusing the board's existing `heldTasks`, `archivedTasks` and `humanTasks`
selectors.

## Work and rationale

The old component was one computed: filter out archived and held, optionally
filter by one status, sort by `updated_at`. That made two product mistakes.
First, the default result set was "everything", so on this repo 1,035 done cards
buried the one review task. Second, the two task classes the board already
surfaced separately — held and human — were invisible on a phone; a held human
task like #0907 could not be reached at all. The URL was also ignored, so
`/work?status=review` (a link desktop honours) landed on "All statuses".

I split the model into four explicit layers:

1. **View (`status`)** — `attention` (default), `all`, `needs`, the six real
   statuses, and `held` / `archived` / `human`. `attention` is a grouping view,
   not a status filter. The parked views use the store selectors directly, so
   the queue and the desktop Human / Archived / Held lists can never disagree
   about what "held" means (flag, `hold` tag or expiry).
2. **Base pool** — the tasks a view starts from. Archived is excluded everywhere
   except its own view; `attention` excludes done. This is where the "done is
   behind a filter" rule lives.
3. **Quick filters and search** — priority, area, story, human assignment and
   the substring search, applied to the pool.
4. **Sections** — grouped views bucket the filtered list into Needs you,
   Review, Active, Ready, Inbox, Draft and (for `all`) Done. A task belongs to
   Needs you when a human is assigned it, it needs input, or a hold is active;
   it is removed from its status bucket so the same card never appears twice.
   Section counts are the bucketed totals; "Show more" reveals 12 more without
   changing the total.

The card list is paginated per section rather than virtualised. With six grouped
sections and a 12-card page, the default view paints at most 72 cards even on a
1,000-task board, and a single-status view paints 12. Virtualisation would have
added scroll-position bookkeeping and made section headers/Show more harder to
keep accessible; a bounded page plus `content-visibility: auto` on list items
gets the acceptance target with far less machinery. Every render-level computed
is a single pass over the pool, so sort/filter toggles are O(n) over 1,000 items.

Search is deliberately narrow: task id (with or without `#`), title, and area,
using the shared `parseTaskAreas` helper that global search also uses for its
area text. The task asked for exactly those fields, so I did not pull in global
search's body/fuzzy scoring — a queue search that matches prose would widen
results when the user is trying to narrow them. The chip options for area and
story are derived from the current board, so they only offer values that exist.

Filter state is written back to the URL with `router.replace`. Replace, not
push, means typing does not stack one history entry per keystroke while reload
and return-from-detail still restore the view. The write preserves unrelated
query parameters (`task`, `tab`), and a second watcher adopts external URL
changes so Back/forward and pasted links work without a reload.

## Approaches tried

I first considered adding "needs attention" as a computed sort (human/needs
input first, then status rank) while keeping one flat list. That would have
satisfied ordering but not the requirement that section counts match rows, and a
long mixed list still hides the boundary between "work now" and "done". Grouped
sections with counts are easier to scan and made the done-hiding rule explicit.

I also considered rendering a single "Done" collapsed section in the default
view. The acceptance criterion is that no done task appears before the
attention work; a collapsed section satisfies the letter of that, but a "Done
1,035" header on a phone is still noise. I left done out of the default view and
gave it both a status option and a place in "All statuses", where it sorts last.

For performance I weighed a virtual scroller. Windowing a variable-height card
list inside a document scroller needs measurement, resize handling and
scroll-anchoring work that would dwarf the feature; pagination achieves the
"about 100 cards" bound deterministically and gives the user an obvious next
action.

## Challenges and blockers

The trickiest part was keeping the URL and local refs in sync without a feedback
loop while still honouring browser navigation. The solution is two watchers: one
compares desired URL params with the route's current ones and only calls
`replace` when they differ; the other adopts the route's params into local
state. Because both settle on the same values, a self-write causes at most one
no-op pass.

The existing test file mocked `useRouter` as a fresh object per call, so URL
writes were unassertable. I made the mock stable, added coverage for
`?status=review`, URL writes, preserved unrelated params, grouped ordering,
search by id/title/area, chips, held/human reachability and the 1,000-task card
cap. The old filtered-empty assertion still passes because the empty heading is
derived from the view label ("No done tasks").

Formatting was the only check failure: oxfmt wanted changes in the two edited
files. `bun run fmt` fixed them and the scoped check went green.

The 1,000-task card bound is enforced and covered by a test. The separate
"under 300ms on a mid-range phone profile" target was not measured in this
session — no throttled mobile browser profile was run — so that figure should be
verified in a browser profile rather than taken as evidence from this report.

## Key learnings

- Reusing the store's `heldTasks` / `humanTasks` selectors is what makes the
  queue and the board tell the same truth; re-deriving "held" in a component
  would have drifted on tags and hold expiry.
- Pagination is an acceptable substitute for virtualisation when the bound is
  part of the acceptance criteria; it is far easier to test and to keep
  accessible.
- A default view is a product decision, not a default value. Naming it
  "Needs attention" and making it a grouping, not a status, is what turns the
  queue from "all 1,065 cards" into "what do I do next".
- URL-owned filter state needs an explicit no-op comparison; relying on router
  identity behaviour makes feedback loops fragile.
